stories.headline: Anthropic makes its IPO filing public, setting up what could be the largest stock debut ever
stories.summary: Anthropic, the company that makes the Claude chatbot, on Monday made public its paperwork to sell shares on the stock market, a step that several outlets say could lead to the biggest initial public offering in history. MarketWatch reports it could pitch investors the week of Nov. 9 and begin trading as soon as the week after. The filing came on a day of very large AI fundraising deals, and European chip stocks rose on Tuesday on what The Wall Street Journal called renewed optimism about AI-linked stocks.
stories.why_it_matters: If the listing goes ahead, anyone with a brokerage account could buy shares in a major AI developer, and how investors receive it will show how much Wall Street is willing to pay for the AI boom.
stories.background: An initial public offering, or IPO, is when a private company first sells shares to the public on a stock exchange. Before it can do that, a U.S. company must file a document called an S-1, or prospectus, with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), laying out its finances, its plans and the risks it faces. Anthropic submitted a draft confidentially in June so regulators could review it privately; Monday's release made it public. The next step is a “roadshow,” in which the company and its banks pitch large investors before a share price is set. The listing comes as big tech companies spend and borrow enormous sums to build the data centers and chips that AI runs on. Disclosure: this brief is written by Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic, so read this story with that in mind and check the linked coverage.

facts.text: The Securities and Exchange Commission released Anthropic's S-1 filing on Monday, Oct. 26.

Anthropic first submitted the paperwork confidentially in June, which let the SEC review its finances before the public release; at the time it said the number of shares and the price had not been set.
Outlets including the Financial Times, NPR, the Associated Press and Axios said the offering could be among the biggest stock market debuts ever, and possibly the biggest.
With the filing public, Anthropic can hold its investor roadshow the week of Nov. 9 and would be eligible to start trading as soon as the following week, MarketWatch reported.

The prospectus includes warnings about AI itself: the BBC reported that Anthropic warned of “catastrophic risk” to humankind, the AP reported the CEO warned of risk to humanity, and CBS News and the South China Morning Post said its section on risks runs 93 pages.
A $63 billion debt deal for Anthropic, announced Monday, is the biggest ever to raise money for AI infrastructure, and Broadcom's CEO intervened to seal it, The Wall Street Journal reported.

Also on Monday, Meta announced plans to raise a total of $95 billion for AI infrastructure, with Nvidia and AMD set to invest $4 billion in Meta, and Meta and SpaceX both moved to raise billions more for AI.
Axios described a $235 billion AI dealmaking blitz led by the Anthropic filing, which it said nearly equals 1% of U.S. economic output (GDP).
European semiconductor stocks rose on Tuesday, which The Wall Street Journal tied to renewed optimism about AI-exposed stocks after the filing.
The New York Times reported that Wall Street banks and chipmakers are among those poised to benefit from the listing.

stories.headline: Fed is expected to hold rates this week, with more hikes possible later
stories.summary: The Federal Reserve's rate-setting committee meets Tuesday and Wednesday, and almost everyone surveyed expects it to leave its benchmark interest rate unchanged after raising it in September for the first time in three years. With inflation moving the wrong way and the job market steady, coverage says the focus is on whether Fed Chair Kevin Warsh signals more increases ahead.
stories.why_it_matters: The Fed's rate sets the tone for what you pay on credit cards, car loans and mortgages and what you earn on savings, so a signal of more hikes means borrowing could get more expensive.
stories.background: The Federal Reserve is the U.S. central bank. Its main tool is the federal funds rate, the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans, which ripples out to the rates people pay and earn. Raising it makes borrowing more expensive, which tends to cool spending and slow price increases; cutting it does the opposite. In September the Fed raised the rate by a quarter of a percentage point (25 “basis points”), to a range of 3.75% to 4%. The latest federal data show consumer prices up 3.7% in the year to September, well above the Fed's 2% goal, with unemployment at 4.2%.

facts.text: The Fed's rate-setting committee meets Oct. 27-28, and officials will announce their decision this week.
In a CNBC survey, 93% of respondents expected the Fed to pause at this week's meeting, and Fox Business and The New York Times reported that the Fed is expected to hold rates steady.
In September the Fed raised its target range by a quarter point to 3.75%-4% in a unanimous vote, saying inflation remained elevated and pointing to its 2% goal.
The September increase was the Fed's first rate hike in three years, CBS News reported.
Kevin Warsh is in his first months as Fed chair.

The New York Times reported that inflation is moving in the wrong direction while the labor market remains stable, which strengthens the case for higher rates, and that Warsh will have to explain why the Fed is holding.
CNBC's survey found respondents expect rate hikes to come later rather than this week.

The Washington Post noted that the Fed generally avoids moving rates right before elections, and looked at the times it did; Fox Business noted this is the Fed's last decision before the midterm elections.

stories.headline: Canada trade talks gain momentum as Trump adjusts tariffs, reports say
stories.summary: Fox Business reported that a U.S.-Canada trade deal is “very close” as President Trump adjusts tariffs on Canadian goods, and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Trump is moving closer to Canada's demands, the Associated Press reported. NBC News said the White House has softened its tone a week before midterm elections in which inflation is a top voter concern. No deal has been announced, and a Honda executive warned that the higher auto tariffs Trump has threatened would be “catastrophic.”
stories.why_it_matters: Tariffs on Canadian cars, parts and aluminum raise costs for U.S. manufacturers that can show up in what you pay for cars and other goods, so a deal, or a breakdown that brings higher tariffs, would reach household budgets.
stories.background: Canada is one of the largest U.S. trading partners, and the two economies are closely tied, especially in cars, energy and metals. A tariff is a tax on imports; the importing company pays it and often passes the cost on to customers. Trump has raised tariffs on Canada several times this year: in July he ordered 50% tariffs on certain Canadian products, and in September he banned imports of some Canadian goods, including dairy products, alcoholic drinks and motorcycles. Carney, Canada's prime minister, has been negotiating with Trump, and the talks continue a week before the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3.

facts.text: Fox Business reported that a Canada trade deal is “very close” as Trump adjusts tariffs, and on Tuesday that Trump is nearing a deal as tariff talks gain steam.
The Center Square reported that Trump is swapping 22 tariffs on Canadian goods for 100 others, with the change taking effect Friday.
Carney said Trump is moving closer to Canada's trade demands as the U.S. midterm elections approach, the Associated Press reported.
The office of Canada's trade minister, Dominic LeBlanc, said Canada remains in “constructive dialogue” with Washington.
Carney said he and Trump discussed “issues around trade” in a phone call on Oct. 21.
NBC News reported that Trump's combative approach to Canada appears to be softening days before midterm elections in which inflation fueled by tariffs is a primary concern for voters.
Axios reported that Trump on Tuesday praised Quebec's new separatist premier, continuing to jab at Ottawa, even as his top economic adviser suggested a deal to ease the trade war is possible.
Trump has threatened to double tariffs on Canadian vehicles and parts from 25% to 50% if no trade deal is reached, CNBC reported.
A Honda executive said higher tariffs on Canadian imports would be “catastrophic” for the auto industry, Reuters and CNBC reported.

The Wall Street Journal reported that the administration's 50% tariff on Canadian aluminum, much of it made at smelters in Quebec that run on cheap hydroelectric power, has pushed up prices for American industry.

In July, Trump ordered 50% tariffs on certain Canadian products, effective Aug. 19, and in September he barred imports of some Canadian goods, including dairy products, alcoholic drinks and motorcycles, starting Sept. 29.

framing.note: Casts Trump as closing in on a deal, with the talks gaining steam.

stories.headline: Boeing shares drop about 10% on slower 737 Max plans and a weaker cash outlook
stories.summary: Boeing's stock fell about 10% on Tuesday after the plane maker reported third-quarter results and said it won't significantly increase 737 Max production until late 2027. Reuters said investors were reacting to slower-than-expected production and a weaker outlook for free cash flow, and MarketWatch said Boeing will come up short on 737 Max deliveries.
stories.why_it_matters: When Boeing builds jets more slowly, airlines wait longer for planes they have already ordered, and the company's results matter to its workers, suppliers and shareholders.
stories.background: Boeing makes commercial airliners, and the pace at which it builds its 737 Max jet is central to its plan to turn the business around. Free cash flow is the cash a company has left after paying its operating costs and investing in factories and equipment; it shows whether a business can fund itself, pay down debt and reward shareholders. Companies report results every three months, and investors often react as much to what a company says about the future, its “outlook,” as to the past quarter. Boeing's backlog, the orders it has taken but not yet filled, is at a record, which means many customers are waiting on it to build planes.

facts.text: Boeing reported its quarterly results before the market opened on Tuesday.
Boeing's stock fell about 10% after the company said it won't significantly ramp up 737 Max production until late 2027.
Reuters reported that shares sold off on slower-than-expected 737 production and a weaker free cash flow outlook.
MarketWatch reported that Boeing will come up short on 737 Max deliveries, which it said casts doubt on Boeing's turnaround plans.
Boeing's results release reported third-quarter operating cash flow of $1.5 billion and free cash flow of $0.5 billion.
Boeing said its order backlog reached a record $745 billion, including more than 6,300 commercial airplanes.
Boeing said two newer versions of the jet, the 737-7 and the 737-10, received amended type certification from the Federal Aviation Administration, the 737-10 in October.

stories.headline: Oil eases on Middle East diplomacy and gold rises as traders await the Fed
stories.summary: Oil futures pulled back on Tuesday as traders focused on diplomatic efforts to ease tensions in the Middle East, and gold settled higher, The Wall Street Journal reported. Softer oil also helped lift European stocks, which shrugged off an earnings miss at HSBC, meaning results that fell short of forecasts, Reuters reported. Prices swung during the day as traders also positioned ahead of the Fed's meeting.
stories.why_it_matters: Oil prices feed directly into what you pay for gasoline, heating and shipped goods, so a lasting drop would ease pressure on household budgets and on the inflation the Fed is trying to bring down.
stories.background: Oil is priced per barrel and traded through futures, contracts to buy or sell at a set price on a future date; the two main benchmarks are U.S. crude (WTI) and Brent, the international benchmark. Prices have been above $100: the latest federal data, from Oct. 20, put U.S. crude near $108 a barrel and Brent near $115. This year oil has swung with the ups and downs of U.S.-Iran peace talks and with risks to tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. Gold is often bought as a place to park money when investors are nervous; because it pays no interest, higher interest rates can make it less attractive.

facts.text: Gold settled higher on Tuesday as oil futures pulled back, with the market focusing on diplomatic efforts to ease tensions in the Middle East.
Reuters reported that gold gained on softer oil prices ahead of the Fed meeting.
European shares shrugged off an HSBC earnings miss as other company results and relief on oil lifted sentiment, Reuters reported.
An earlier Reuters item on Canadian stock futures described the opposite moves, with gold weakness offsetting oil gains, a sign of how prices swung during the day.
In August, oil rose as hopes for a U.S.-Iran peace deal faded amid risks around the Strait of Hormuz, and dipped on news of progress in talks over the strait.
